summary: Gives the results of a survey describing available X.500 implementations, both commercial and openly available. It is a revision of RFC 1292. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 2116.

eli5.summary: A shopping list of programs that run an electronic directory. A newer list replaced it.

subtitle: A survey of X.500 directory system implementations and their capabilities.

tldr.problem: Organizations need to understand what X.500 implementations are available and what features they provide before deploying directory services.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs 26 X.500 implementations (DSAs, DUAs, and DUA interfaces), describing their features, platforms, conformance to standards, and interoperability.
tldr.outcome: Provides a reference guide for those evaluating X.500 technology for directory service deployment.

today: RFC 1632 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 2116, which provides an updated catalog. The X.500 protocol and directory services remain important, though LDAP has become the dominant directory access protocol.

sections.title: Introduction to X.500
sections.content:
This RFC catalogs currently available implementations of X.500, the OSI Application Layer Directory standard. The document includes both commercial products and openly available offerings, representing the results of a survey that updated RFC 1292.

X.500 implementations are classified into three categories: DSAs (Directory System Agents that provide directory functionality), DUAs (Directory User Agents that let users access the Directory), and DUA Interfaces (lightweight clients that support a subset of DUA functionality or use protocols other than DAP).

The document contains detailed descriptions of 26 implementations, allowing readers to identify products that meet their criteria for directory service deployment.
sections.eli5: This is a list of programs that run an electronic directory, divided into three types: big directory servers, programs for looking things up in the directory, and simple tools that do basic lookups.

sections.title: Keywords and Implementation Types
sections.content:
The RFC uses a comprehensive keyword system to organize implementations across eight functional categories. Keywords describe Availability (commercially available, free, via FTP), Conformance to Internet standards (RFC-1274, RFC-1485, RFC-1487), Implementation Type (DSA Only, DSA/DUA, DUA Interface, LDAP), Internetworking Environment (OSI Transport, RFC-1006 with TCP/IP, X.25), and Pilot Connectivity (DUA or DSA connectivity to the experimental Internet Directory pilot).

Additional categories cover Operating Environment (hardware platforms like Sun, DEC, IBM) and miscellaneous features (X Window System, Motif user interface, requirements for ISODE).
sections.eli5: Each product is tagged with keywords that describe what it costs, what standards it follows, what type of directory tool it is, what computers it runs on, and what special features it has.

sections.title: Implementation Descriptions
sections.content:
The RFC provides standardized descriptions for each of the 26 implementations, covering Name and responsible organization, Keywords characterizing the product, Abstract describing the application and its pilot projects, Compliance with CCITT X.500-X.521 recommendations and NIST agreements, Conformance with Internet standards, and Consistence with informational RFCs.

Each description also documents Interoperability with other X.500 implementations, Pilot Connectivity to the experimental Internet Directory, Known Bugs, Caveats and Limitations, Internetworking Environment (protocols and transports), Hardware and Software Platforms required, Availability terms, and the Date Last Updated.
sections.eli5: For each product, the document tells you its name, what special features it has, how it works, what computers it runs on, whether it costs money, and who to contact for more information.

sections.title: Implementation Diversity
sections.content:
The implementations surveyed demonstrate substantial diversity. Some are commercial products from vendors including Bull, DEC, HP, and IBM; others are freely available from universities and research institutions (such as QUIPU from ISODE and LDAP implementations). Implementations vary widely in scope: some provide only DSA or DUA functionality, while others combine both; some add LDAP interfaces for simpler access.

Platforms range from traditional Unix systems (Sun, DEC ULTRIX, IBM RISC) to personal computers (IBM PC, Macintosh) and specialized hardware (Bull DPX/2, Tandem systems). Networking environments include OSI protocols (X.25, TP4), TCP/IP with RFC-1006, and combinations supporting both.
sections.eli5: The products come from different companies and work on different computers. Some are expensive and some are free. They all do similar jobs but use different methods and run on different machines.
